paragraphs.text:
[?] Of Gregory of Nyssa, our father among the saints: On the Goal That Accords with God and on True Asceticism; addressed to the ascetics who asked about the goal of piety; and an outline of how they ought to live together and strive together. [?]

Suppose someone draws his mind a little away from the body, gets free of the slavery and folly of the passions, and looks at his own soul with clear and honest reasoning. He will see plainly in its nature both God's love for us and the purpose of God's creation. Examining it in this way, he will find that the impulse of desire toward what is good and best shares man's very being and has grown up together with him. He will also find, joined to his nature, a dispassionate and blessed love for that intelligible and blessed image of which man is a copy. But these visible things, which are always flowing away, lead the soul astray through irrational passion and bitter pleasure. They deceive and bewitch the soul that is careless and left unguarded through [?] indolence, and drag it toward terrible vice, which is born of the pleasures of life and gives birth to death for those who love it. For this reason the grace of our Savior has given the knowledge of the truth, the saving medicine for souls, to those who receive it with longing. By it the deception that bewitches man is undone, and the dishonorable mind of the flesh is extinguished, as the soul is guided by the light of truth toward the Divine, with which it has received union, and toward its own salvation. So whoever means to bring soul and body to God according to the law of piety, and to offer him bloodless and pure worship, must make the pious faith the guide of his life, the faith that the voices of the saints cry out to us throughout Scripture. In this way he must give over his soul, obedient and responsive to the rein, to the race-courses of virtue. He must loose himself from the bonds of this life and become wholly devoted to faith and to the life of God alone, knowing clearly that wherever there is the faith of piety and a blameless life, the power of Christ is present too; and wherever the power of Christ is, there is escape from vice.

Great indeed, great is holy baptism for gaining the goods of the spirit, for those who receive it with fear. The Spirit is rich and generous and always flows to those who receive grace. The holy apostles were filled with this Spirit and displayed the fruits of that fullness to the churches of Christ. This same Spirit stays as fellow-worker and companion with those who have sincerely received the gift, according to the measure of faith of each who has shared in it, and builds up in each the good that leads the soul to zeal in the works of faith. So each of us must always advance through virtue and bring himself forward toward the perfect man, as the Apostle says: "Until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." The body's growth in height is not in our power at all, for nature does not measure size by a person's will and pleasure but by its own impulse and necessity. But the soul's stature and beauty in the renewal of birth, which the grace of the Spirit gives through the zeal of the one who receives it, depend on our own will. As far as you extend your struggles for piety, so far the soul's stature extends with them. The grace of the Spirit gives eternal life and unspeakable joy in heaven. But worthiness to receive the gifts and to enjoy the grace belongs to the love for labors that comes through faith. When righteousness of works and the grace of the Spirit come together in the same soul, together they fill it with blessed life. Separated from each other, they bring the soul no gain. For the grace of God cannot visit souls that run away from salvation, and the power of human virtue is not enough by itself to raise souls that have no share in grace to the form of life. "Unless the Lord builds the house and guards the city, those who labor at them labor in vain." From this we learn not to suppose that the whole crown rests on human efforts, but to refer our hopes for the outcome to the will of God. And God's will is to purify the soul through grace and bring it pure to God. Such people the Lord calls blessed, saying: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Do you see the prize of purity? What is better than to see God, as far as that is possible for us? That is why David asks for this, saying: "Let my heart be blameless in your statutes, so that I may not be put to shame." He bids us fear shame, and bids us put it off like a soiled garment. And again he says: "Then I shall not be put to shame, when I look upon all your commandments." For the Spirit grants boldness in the fulfilling of the commandments. And again: "Create a clean heart in me, O God," and "Establish me with a guiding spirit." Elsewhere

he asks: "Who shall go up to the mountain of the Lord?" Then he answers: "One who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart." Whoever wants to become close to someone must imitate that person's way of life. So the soul that longs to become the bride of Christ must be made like the beauty of Christ as far as it can. The soul that means to fly up to the Divine and cleave to Christ must drive every sin out of itself. I mean theft, robbery, adultery, greed, fornication, the disease of the tongue, and every visible kind of sin. I also mean the hidden ones: envy, unbelief, malice, deceit, and the whole festering swarm of vice, which Scripture hates and abhors as much as the open kinds of sin. Whose bones has the Lord scattered? Is it not those of the men-pleasers? Whom does the Lord abhor as accursed and murderous? Is it not the treacherous and deceitful man? "For the Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit." Does not David openly curse those who speak peace with their neighbors but have evil in their hearts? That is why we are commanded neither to chase after praise from men nor to be ashamed of dishonor from them. Scripture deprives those who practise some virtue for show of the rewards in heaven, since they receive the praise of men here. But they say: "Then how can the Lord say, 'Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven'?" We answer that the word commands whoever follows God's commandments to do everything he does with his eyes on God, and to please him alone, hunting for no glory from men. He should flee their praise and all display, yet become known to everyone through his life and works. And note that the Lord did not say that those who see these works should admire the one displaying them, but that they should "glorify your Father in heaven." He bids all glory be referred to the Father, and every action be completed according to the Father's will, for the reward for the works of virtue is stored up with him. Reach for the praise from above, saying with David: "My praise is with you." And: "In the Lord shall be praised

[?] they did not see fit," he says, "to keep God in their knowledge, he gave them up to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting. They are filled with every kind of unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, greed and malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit and malignity. They are whisperers, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, faithless, heartless, implacable, merciless. Though they know God's decree, that those who do such things deserve death." Do you see how he ranked malignity, arrogance, deceit and the other hidden sins together with murder, greed and all such things? The evils hidden in souls are so wicked and so hard to cure that human effort and virtue alone cannot rub them out and destroy them, unless one takes the power of the Spirit as an ally. That is why David says: "Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others." For each human being is fitted together from two parts, soul and body. The body is the outward part, while the soul remains within throughout life. So a person must keep watch over the outward part, guarding against some dangerous sin falling on it and shaking and corrupting it. About this the Apostle warns: "If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him." And he must guard the inward part with all vigilance, so that no thought of vice rises from the depths and corrupts the reasoning of piety, filling the soul with passions that secretly tear it apart and so enslaving it. "You shall not yoke together on your threshing floor animals of different kinds," says blessed Moses, "such as an ox and an ass. Nor shall you weave wool together with linen in a garment. You shall not grow two crops together in the field of your land, nor a second crop in the same year." You shall not mate an animal of one kind with another for breeding. What do these riddles mean? That we must not plant vice and virtue together in the same soul. What friendship can self-control have with self-indulgence? What agreement can righteousness have with unrighteousness? One always gives way to the other. So the wise farmer must send out the streams of his life pure, as if from a good spring of drinking water. He must know only God's crops, labor at them all his life, and persevere with them. Then, even if some alien thought springs up in the hidden places of virtue, the One who sees everything will see your labors and quickly cut out, by his own power, the festering root of such thoughts before it sprouts. It is impossible for one who constantly waits on God to miss his hope or be left without vindication. Consider the widow in the Gospel. She brought the great injustice done to her before a judge who did not love mankind. Yet her great diligence and persistence in pleading overcame the judge's character and stirred him to punish the one who had wronged her. Do not, then, give up when you pray. For if

her shameless persistence in pleading swayed the mind of a merciless ruler, how can we give up our zeal toward God? Do you not know that mercy often comes before people even ask? "Strive eagerly," says the Apostle, "for the spiritual gifts; and yet I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal." He shows what love gains in the following words: "Love does not envy, does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own, is not provoked, keeps no account of evil, does not rejoice in unrighteousness but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails." What does this mean? A person may obtain the other gifts the Spirit provides: kinds of tongues, I mean, and prophecy, and knowledge, and gifts of healing. But if he has not yet been cleanly set free, by the Spirit's help, from the passions that trouble him within, and has not received into his soul the perfect medicine of salvation, he still stands in fear of falling. He lacks the love that supports him and keeps him firm in the steadfastness of virtue. So when the wealth that comes from that prayer reaches you, then become poor in mind. Always humble yourself, and wait in your soul for the good of love as a kind of foundation for the treasure of grace. Struggle against every passion until you reach the goal of piety. Again the Apostle says: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away." By "new creation" he meant the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in a heart that is pure and blameless and freed from all vice, wickedness and shame. When the soul hates sinning, and makes itself at home as far as it can in the life of virtue, and, transformed in its way of living, receives the grace of the Spirit into itself, it has become entirely new and has been created again. The sayings "Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump" and "Let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" also agree with what is said about the new creation. For the pirate sets many snares for the soul, and human nature by itself is too weak to win the victory over him. That is why the Apostle bids us arm our limbs with heavenly weapons, the breastplate of righteousness, saying: "Put it on, and shoe your feet with the readiness of peace, and gird your loins with truth. And above all, the [?]" [?]

Such, then, is the goal of piety. Those who have chosen the life of philosophy must know precisely how they may all cast off self-will and pride in their achievements. Denying their own soul together with this life, they must look to one wealth only: the prize God has given to those who love him, as the reward of love for Christ. As the same Apostle says: "Let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith." Let us not, then, be puffed up by the gifts of the Spirit. Let us not take some virtuous achievement as an excuse for thinking highly of ourselves and putting on airs before we reach the end of what we hope for. Otherwise we may fall from our course, having made our earlier labor useless to ourselves through self-will, and be shown unworthy of the perfection toward which the grace of the Spirit was drawing us. This is a great achievement of philosophy: that one who is great . . . [?] for to those . . . [?] in heart, and to condemn his own life, not having in his conscience the sense that he has made himself worthy of God. We think enough has been said about the hope of the goal for those who choose to live as philosophers. It remains to add how such people ought to live with one another, and how they should run together until they reach the city above. Whoever sincerely disdains the honors of this life and renounces all glory here below must deny his own soul along with this life. Denial of the soul means never seeking one's own will but the will of God. It means using that will as a good helmsman, who steers the whole community of the brotherhood in harmony toward the harbor of the divine will. It also means owning nothing apart from the common stock except the garment that covers the body. In this way it will be easier to carry out eagerly, with pleasure and hope, whatever the superiors command, as a slave of Christ, bought for the common need of the brothers. This is what the Lord wants, when he says: "Whoever among you wishes to be first and great, let him be last of all and servant of all." Such service must go unpaid by men. One who serves in this way ought to be subject to all, and to serve the brothers like a debtor paying off a loan. The superiors of this spiritual choir, too, must consider how great their responsibility is and reckon with the tricks of the vice that lies in wait for faith. They must struggle in a way worthy of their office and not let their minds be lifted up by their authority. In their office the superiors must labor more than the others, think more humbly than those under them, and offer their own lives as a pattern of servanthood [?]

to the others, regarding those entrusted to them as a deposit held from God. So the superiors must care for the brothers like good tutors caring for young children entrusted to them by their fathers. Such tutors watch the children's habits and give blows to one, a warning to another, praise to another, and something else of the kind to another, doing nothing out of favor or dislike toward them. This is how spiritual superiors ought to act as well. Suppose you behave this way toward one another, those under authority and those who teach: the first obeying commands with joy, the others gladly leading the brothers toward perfection, and all outdoing one another in showing honor. Then you will live the life of angels on earth. Let each one convince himself that he is inferior not only to the brother who lives with him [?] but to every human being. Whoever knows this will truly be a disciple of Christ. Since you know the fruits of humility and the damage done by conceit, imitate the Master. Advance toward the calling above as one body and one [soul], loving God and one another. For love and fear toward the Lord are the first fulfillment of the law. Yet love for God does not naturally grow in us simply or on its own. It comes through many labors and great efforts, and with the cooperation of Christ, as Wisdom has said: "If you seek her like silver and search for her as for treasures, then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God." Once you have found the knowledge of God, you will easily understand fear as well and achieve the next thing, loving your neighbor. When the first and great thing has been gained, the second, being lesser, takes less labor. After all, how could someone who does not love God with his whole heart and his whole mind care soundly and honestly for love of the brothers? [?] When the craftsman of vice finds someone who does not give his whole soul to God and has not poured himself out in love for him, he easily overpowers him, tripping him up with evil thoughts. Sometimes he makes the commands of Scripture seem heavy and service to the brothers a burden. At other times he lifts him up to boastfulness and conceit over that very service to his fellow servants [?], so that he seeks glory from men and begs honor from the brothers. In this way he busies himself with the business of unbelievers and does their deeds. For whoever hunts for human honors instead of heavenly ones is an unbeliever, as the Lord himself says somewhere: "How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?" So when the love of God is present in us, [?] the rest must follow along with it: brotherly love, gentleness, sincerity, perseverance and zeal in prayer, and in short every virtue. But since this possession is great, great

…labours are needed to acquire it: labours undertaken not to show off before people, but to please God, who knows what is hidden. For those who love God the labour of keeping the commandments is easy and sweet, because love for him makes the struggle light and delightful to us. That is why the Evil One strives in every way to drive the fear of the Lord out of our souls, and to break up our love for him with lawless pleasures. For if he finds the guards careless, he is skilled at seizing his chance, slipping in among the labours of virtue, and sowing his tares among the wheat: I mean abuse, conceit, vainglory, the desire for honour, and the other things wickedness produces. We must therefore stay awake and watch for the Enemy on every side, so that even if he shamelessly brings some scheme against us, it may be beaten back before it touches the soul. Keep remembering this too, I beg you. Abel offered the Lord a sacrifice from the firstborn of his sheep and from their fat, while Cain offered from the fruits of the earth but not from the sheep. “And God looked,” it says, “on the sacrifices of Abel, but to the gifts of Cain he paid no heed.” So we can learn from this story that whatever is done with fear and faith pleases the Lord, and not what is done lavishly but without love. Abraham too received the blessing from Melchizedek in no other way than by bringing the firstfruits and the choicest things to the priest of God. By “the choicest things” and “the best of one's possessions” Scripture means the soul itself and the mind. It bids us not to offer God our praises and prayers in a stingy way, nor to bring the Master whatever comes to hand, but to dedicate to God whatever is choicest in the soul, or rather the whole soul itself. As for the parts of virtue, though, it is impossible to say which should be counted the best and practised before the others, which comes second, and so on down the list. For they all hold on to one another equally, and through one another they lead those who practise them up to the summit. Simplicity hands a person on to obedience; obedience to faith; faith to hope; hope to righteousness; righteousness to service; service to humility; from humility gentleness takes him over; gentleness leads him to joy; joy to love; love to prayer. So, linked to one another and drawing along whoever holds on to them, they lead him up to the very summit of what he longs for. In just the opposite way, wickedness drags its friends down through its own parts to the lowest depths of evil. But we must persevere above all in prayer. Prayer is like the leader of the chorus of the virtues, and through a mystical holiness, a spiritual working and an ineffable disposition it joins to God the one who perseveres in it. Such a person burns with longing and never has his fill of prayer, but is always found longing for the good, as it is said: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still.” And elsewhere: “You have put gladness in my heart.” And the Lord says: “The kingdom of

heaven is within you.” By “kingdom” he meant the gladness that comes into souls from above through the Spirit. This gladness is a pledge of the eternal joy that the souls of the saints will one day enjoy. It has now been shown what the aim of godliness is, the aim that must be set before those who choose the life that is dear to God: the cleansing of the soul, and the indwelling of the Spirit as one advances through good works. So let each of you prepare his soul in the way shown and fill it with divine love, and then give himself to prayers and fasts, remembering the one who urges us to pray without ceasing and not to lose heart. For eagerness in prayer brings us great gifts. Only let each of you pray with an intent and [?] conscience, never letting his mind wander on purpose, and not paying it as an unwilling debt forced on him, but fulfilling the love and longing of his soul. The Lord himself will also teach those who ask how they ought to pray, as it is said: “He who gives prayer to the one who prays.” So one must ask, and the one who perseveres in prayer must know that in so great an undertaking he has to fight the contest with great eagerness and strength. For wickedness lies in wait especially for such people, seeking from every side to overturn their eagerness. From one side comes slackness of body and soul; from the other, softness, listlessness, negligence and the rest, by which the soul is carried off bit by bit and destroyed, and deserts to its enemy. Reason must therefore stand over the soul like a wise helmsman, getting it ready to sail straight to the harbour above and handing the soul back unharmed to God who entrusted it to him. The superiors too must help such a person, and with all eagerness and admonition nourish the desire of the one who prays for the goal he has set himself. For when the fruit of the virtues in those who truly pray is displayed to those who understand, it benefits not only the one who has advanced, but also those who are still infants and in need of teaching, and it urges them to imitate what they see. The fruits of sincere prayer are simplicity, love, humility, endurance, guilelessness and the like. Before the eternal fruits come, these spring up here and now in the life of the earnest person. Prayer is adorned with these fruits; without them its labour is in vain. And this is true not of prayer alone but of every path of the philosophic life: if it bears such growth, it truly is a path of righteousness and leads to a right end, but if it is stripped of them, it is left an empty name. What use is a vine that has been laboured over if there is no fruit, the very thing for which the farmer endured the labour? What gain is there in fasting, prayer and vigils if peace, joy and love are absent, together with the other fruits of the grace of the Spirit? So we must endure the labours of fasting and prayer and the other works with great pleasure, love and hope, but we must believe that the flowers and fruits of these labours come from the working of the Spirit.

If anyone credits these things to himself and attributes everything to his own labours, then in place of those pure fruits a spirit of arrogance grows in him. So we must endure the struggles for virtue with pleasure, but credit God with freeing the soul from the passions. The soul will then rise above itself and above the Enemy's most powerful wickedness, and offer itself as a good dwelling for the worshipful and Holy Spirit. From the Spirit it receives the immortal peace of Christ, and through that peace it is joined to the Lord and clings to him. Some, however, do not yet have the intensity of the highest prayer, nor the eagerness and strength the task demands, and so they fall short of this virtue. Let them fulfil their obedience in other things: serving as far as they can, working willingly, and ministering earnestly and with pleasure. Let them do it not for any reward, nor for human glory, nor as though they were serving bodies and souls that are strangers to us, but as servants of Christ, as our own flesh and blood, so that our work may be shown to the Lord as pure and sincere. Let no one plead weakness as an excuse for lacking eagerness in good works, for God commands nothing impossible. “Whoever,” he says, “gives a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.” What could be easier than this commandment? Yet the reward for this easy deed is heavenly. And again: “Whatever you did to one of these, you did to me.” The command is small, but what obedience gains is great. So he demands nothing beyond our strength. Whether what you do is small or great, the reward follows you according to your intention. If it is done in the name and fear of God, the gift comes splendid and can never be taken away. But if it is done for show, listen to the Lord himself declaring on oath: “Truly I tell you, they have their reward.” So that no one may suffer this, he instructs the disciples, and through them us: “Take care not to do your almsgiving, or your praying, or your fasting in front of people; otherwise you have no reward from your Father in heaven.” To him be glory for ever. Amen.
